title: Did Early Humans Keep Souvenirs 500,000 Years Ago?
paragraphs: Few of us think twice about keeping a pebble from a favourite beach or a ticket from a memorable concert. According to a paper in Evolutionary Anthropology, however, humans may have been collecting keepsakes as early as half a million years ago, long before art or writing existed.

The authors, from Tel Aviv University and Oxford University, draw on finds from sites in Israel. At Qesem Cave, small, colourful pebbles were brought in from elsewhere, although no practical purpose has been identified for them. Older, weathered flint tools were also preserved with much of their original surface intact, and in the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were shaped around fossils or unusual patterns in the flint. The researchers suggest that such objects acted as an external memory device, prompting recollection of places and events, and that this may have helped people distinguish their own experiences from stories they had merely heard.

The conclusions should be read with caution. The authors themselves present the idea as a hypothesis rather than proof, and they stress that not every unusual stone was necessarily a keepsake. Because the objects cannot explain their own meaning, the interpretation will always depend on the researchers' reasoning rather than on direct evidence of what these people intended.

questions.q: What was unusual about the pebbles at Qesem Cave?
questions.a: They were colourful, brought from elsewhere and had no identified practical use.

questions.q: What function do the authors propose for keepsakes?
questions.a: An external memory device that helps people recall places and events.

questions.q: Why should the conclusions be treated carefully?
questions.a: The authors present them as a hypothesis, and the objects cannot reveal what people intended.
